passages.t: Come near to listen, and let your words be few
passages.happening:
For the first time the Teacher gives the reader direct commands. ‘Guard your steps when you go to the house of God. Draw near to listen rather than to offer the sacrifice of fools, who do not know that they do wrong’ (verse 1).

“Do not be quick to speak, and do not be hasty in your heart to utter a word before God. After all, God is in heaven and you are on earth. So let your words be few” (verse 2). ‘As a dream comes through many cares, so the speech of a fool comes with many words’ (verse 3).

‘When you make a vow to God, do not delay in fulfilling it, because He takes no pleasure in fools. Fulfill your vow’ (verse 4). ‘It is better not to vow than to make a vow and not fulfill it’ (verse 5). Do not let your mouth lead you into sin, and do not tell the messenger it was a mistake (verse 6). ‘For as many dreams bring futility, so do many words. Therefore, fear God’ (verse 7).
passages.hearers:
In Hebrew Bibles verse 1 of this chapter is numbered 4:17, so the verse numbers in Hebrew run one behind the English.

The sacrifice of fools is worship without a listening heart, a concern that runs through the prophets. In Hebrew, to listen also means to obey.

A vow in Israel was a promise to God, freely made, often in a time of need: if God answered, the person would give an offering or do some act. No one had to make a vow, but once it was spoken it was binding. The Teacher's warning closely follows the law in Deuteronomy. The messenger of verse 6 is probably a temple official or priest who came to collect what had been promised. Some take the messenger to be an angel.

Verses 3 and 7 pair dreams and words. As busy days bring restless dreams, so fools bring many words, and both are hevel, breath. The section ends with the book's great command: fear God.
passages.later: The law says, ‘If you refrain from making a vow, you will not be guilty’ (Deuteronomy 23:22). And James gives the same counsel as verse 2: ‘Everyone should be quick to listen, slow to speak, and slow to anger’ (James 1:19).
passages.asks: God is in heaven and you are on earth, so let your words be few. Ask how much of your prayer is talking and how much is listening. And ask whether there is a promise you made to God that you have quietly let go.

passages.t: Officials over officials, and money that never satisfies
passages.happening:
If you see the poor oppressed and justice denied in the province, do not be astonished, ‘for one official is watched by a superior, and others higher still are over them’ (verse 8). Even the king profits from the fields (verse 9).

‘He who loves money is never satisfied by money, and he who loves wealth is never satisfied by income. This too is futile’ (verse 10). When goods increase, so do those who eat them (verse 11). ‘The sleep of the worker is sweet, whether he eats little or much, but the abundance of the rich man permits him no sleep’ (verse 12).

The Teacher has seen ‘wealth hoarded to the harm of its owner’ (verse 13), and wealth lost in a bad venture, so that there is nothing left for a son (verse 14). ‘As a man came from his mother’s womb, so he will depart again, naked as he arrived. He takes nothing for his labor to carry in his hands’ (verse 15).
passages.hearers:
The word for province in verse 8, medinah, was a common word for an administrative district in the Persian period, often used in Esther, Ezra and Nehemiah, though it also appears in the story of Ahab. Scholars who date the book later read the verse as a picture of an imperial bureaucracy where each layer took its share. Those who hold to Solomon's authorship point out that Solomon also divided Israel into districts under officials. Either way the farmer at the bottom has little recourse.

Most people did hard physical work, and they knew the worker's sweet sleep. The rich man lies awake guarding his goods.

Verse 15 echoes Job's words when he lost everything. Nothing earned can be carried past death.
passages.later: Job said, ‘Naked I came from my mother’s womb, and naked I will return’ (Job 1:21). Paul says it too: ‘For we brought nothing into the world, so we cannot carry anything out of it’ (1 Timothy 6:7).
passages.hard:
Does the Teacher tell people not to be surprised by injustice, as if to accept it?

Verse 8 says that when you see the poor oppressed and justice denied, you should not be astonished, because every official has a superior over him.

Some read this as weary realism: corruption runs all the way up the chain, and each layer protects the one below. Others read it as partial reassurance, that officials are watched and answerable, and they read verse 9 as saying that even the king depends on the land and so has a stake in its care. The Hebrew of verse 9 is difficult, and both readings have defenders.

Either way, the Teacher is not approving oppression. He has already wept over the tears of the oppressed (4:1), and the book's conclusion, that God will judge every deed (12:14), means the injustice he describes is not the last word. His point is that no one should be naive about power.
passages.asks: The lover of money is never satisfied. Ask what number would finally be enough for you, and whether that number keeps moving. And ask whether there is injustice you have learned to shrug at, when the Teacher only asks you not to be surprised by it.

passages.t: Good and fitting: the gift of enjoyment
passages.happening:
‘Here is what I have seen to be good and fitting: to eat and drink, and to find satisfaction in all the labor one does under the sun during the few days of life that God has given him’ (verse 18).

God gives some people riches and wealth, and he enables them to enjoy them, to accept their lot and to rejoice in their work. ‘This is a gift from God’ (verse 19). ‘For a man seldom considers the days of his life, because God keeps him occupied with the joy of his heart’ (verse 20).
passages.hearers:
After the warnings about money, the chapter ends with the counterweight. The same God who sets these limits also gives food, work and the power to enjoy them. Lot, or portion, cheleq, is the share God hands each person.

The last verse is uncertain in Hebrew. It may mean that God keeps a person so busy with joy that the shortness of life does not weigh on him. Or it may mean that God answers a person through the joy of the heart.

The next chapter takes up the darker case: a man who has everything and is not allowed to enjoy it.
passages.later: Paul writes of ‘God, who richly provides all things for us to enjoy’ (1 Timothy 6:17). And Moses reminded Israel where wealth comes from: ‘But remember that it is the LORD your God who gives you the power to gain wealth’ (Deuteronomy 8:18).
passages.asks: The power to enjoy is itself a gift. Ask what good thing you have that you have been too worried to enjoy. And ask God to let you receive today's work and food with a glad heart.
